did_you_know.text: Did you know? The famine during David’s reign lasted three consecutive years, year after year. David sought the Lord, and he was told that the famine was connected with Saul’s family and his attack on the Gibeonites.

Did you know? The Gibeonites are described as not being Israelites, but as a remnant of the Amorites. Nevertheless, the Israelites had sworn an oath to them, and Saul had tried to destroy them in his zeal for Israel and Judah.
Did you know? The Gibeonites did not ask for silver or gold, but for seven men descended from Saul, so that they could be impaled at Gibeah of Saul before the Lord. David agreed to their request.

Did you know? David spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan son of Saul, and did not hand him over to the Gibeonites, because of the oath that David and Jonathan had sworn to each other before the Lord.

Did you know? Rizpah daughter of Aiah guarded the bodies of those who had been impaled from the beginning of the barley harvest until rain fell from the heavens. She did not let the birds approach them by day or the wild animals by night.

Did you know? After the bones of Saul, Jonathan, and those who had been impaled were buried in the tomb of Kish’s family, it is stated: “And God answered the land.” In this chapter, the burial is presented as an act that preceded God’s response to the land.

Did you know? When David grew tired in battle and his life was in danger, Abishai son of Zeruiah struck down the Philistine and saved him. After this, David’s men swore that he would no longer go out to battle, so that he would not extinguish the “lamp of Israel.”

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, four Philistine warriors descended from Rapha are listed as having fallen at the hands of David and his servants. One of them is described as having six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—twenty-four digits in all.
